questions.prompt: Which sequence follows inhaled air towards the gas-exchange surfaces?
options: Trachea → bronchi → bronchioles → alveoli
Alveoli → bronchioles → bronchi → trachea
Trachea → alveoli → bronchi → bronchioles
Bronchioles → trachea → alveoli → bronchi
questions.explanation: The trachea branches into bronchi, then smaller bronchioles, which lead to the alveoli.

questions.prompt: What is the trachea commonly called?
options: The food pipe
The windpipe
The diaphragm
The chest wall
questions.explanation: The trachea is the windpipe, the airway leading from the throat towards the bronchi.

questions.prompt: What are alveoli?
options: Muscles that pull the ribs upwards
Blood vessels that carry blood from the lungs
Tiny air sacs where gases are exchanged with the blood
Rings of cartilage that support the trachea
questions.explanation: Alveoli are microscopic air sacs surrounded by capillaries. They form the main gas-exchange surface.

questions.prompt: Where is the diaphragm found?
options: Inside the trachea
Between the left atrium and ventricle
At the end of every alveolus
Below the lungs, separating the chest from the abdomen
questions.explanation: The diaphragm is a sheet of muscle forming the floor of the thoracic cavity.

questions.prompt: What is the main role of cartilage in the trachea?
options: To help keep the airway open
To pump air into the blood
To carry most oxygen around the body
To digest dust trapped in mucus
questions.explanation: Cartilage supports the tracheal wall so the airway does not easily collapse during breathing.

questions.prompt: How does the nose help prepare inhaled air?
options: It removes all nitrogen from the air
It warms, moistens and helps filter the air
It turns carbon dioxide into oxygen
It makes the air completely free of every pathogen
questions.explanation: The nasal passages warm and moisten air, while hairs and mucus trap some particles. This is not perfect sterilisation.

questions.prompt: What is the main function of the epiglottis during swallowing?
options: To exchange oxygen with capillaries
To flatten the diaphragm
To help prevent food entering the airway
To keep the pulmonary valve open
questions.explanation: The epiglottis helps cover the laryngeal opening during swallowing, reducing the chance of food entering the trachea.

questions.prompt: Which statement about the bronchi is correct?
options: They carry blood from the heart to the lungs
They are the only muscles used in breathing
They join the lungs directly to the stomach
The two main bronchi carry air from the trachea into the lungs
questions.explanation: The trachea divides into a right and left main bronchus, carrying air into the corresponding lung.

questions.prompt: Why does air travelling through a bronchus not yet mean that oxygen has entered the blood?
options: Oxygen must reach a gas-exchange surface and diffuse across it
Blood is absent from the entire chest
Bronchi convert oxygen into carbon dioxide before it reaches alveoli
Oxygen enters blood only through the mouth
questions.explanation: Conducting airways move air. Most oxygen transfer to blood occurs across the alveolar-capillary barrier.

questions.prompt: A blockage in a small bronchiole would most directly reduce what?
options: The number of chambers in the heart
Ventilation of the alveoli supplied by that airway
All oxygen in the surrounding atmosphere
Glucose production in every body cell
questions.explanation: A narrowed or blocked bronchiole restricts airflow to the alveoli beyond it, reducing their ventilation.

questions.prompt: What happens to the diaphragm during a normal inhalation?
options: It relaxes and becomes more domed
It contracts and moves upwards into the chest
It contracts and moves downwards, becoming flatter
It turns into an air-filled balloon
questions.explanation: When the diaphragm contracts it flattens, increasing the volume of the thoracic cavity.

questions.prompt: During normal inhalation, what happens to chest volume?
options: It decreases
It stays exactly constant
It falls to zero
It increases
questions.explanation: Diaphragm contraction and rib movement increase the volume of the chest during inhalation.

questions.prompt: Why does air move into the lungs during inhalation?
options: Pressure inside the lungs becomes slightly lower than atmospheric pressure
Oxygen actively pulls itself through the mouth
The lungs create a permanent vacuum
Atmospheric pressure falls below lung pressure
questions.explanation: Air flows down a pressure gradient. Increasing lung volume makes internal pressure slightly lower than atmospheric pressure.

questions.prompt: During quiet exhalation, what normally happens to the diaphragm?
options: It contracts and flattens further
It relaxes and moves upwards into a more domed shape
It pumps blood towards the heart
It remains maximally contracted
questions.explanation: Relaxation allows the diaphragm to rise as the lungs and chest recoil, reducing lung volume.

questions.prompt: What do the external intercostal muscles do during inhalation?
options: They relax to pull the ribs down and in
They close the alveoli to all airflow
They contract, helping move the ribs up and out
They pump oxygen directly into red blood cells
questions.explanation: Contraction of the external intercostal muscles raises and expands the rib cage, helping increase chest volume.

questions.prompt: Which pressure change is associated with air flowing out during exhalation?
options: Pressure inside the lungs becomes lower than atmospheric pressure
Atmospheric pressure must become zero
Lung pressure stays lower than outside pressure throughout
Pressure inside the lungs becomes slightly greater than atmospheric pressure
questions.explanation: Reducing lung volume increases pressure above atmospheric pressure, driving air out.

questions.prompt: Why is quiet exhalation usually described as largely passive?
options: Elastic recoil helps air leave after inspiratory muscles relax
No pressure difference exists during exhalation
The diaphragm contracts more strongly than during inhalation
Alveoli actively pump every air molecule out
questions.explanation: In quiet breathing, relaxation of inspiratory muscles and elastic recoil usually produce exhalation without strong additional muscle contraction.

questions.prompt: What is tidal volume?
options: The number of breaths in one minute
The volume of air moved in or out during one normal breath
The maximum amount of blood in a lung
The amount of oxygen in the atmosphere
questions.explanation: Tidal volume measures the air volume of an ordinary breath. It is different from breathing rate.

questions.prompt: In a sealed bell-jar lung model, the rubber sheet is pulled down. Why do the balloons inflate?
options: The rubber sheet forces air directly into the balloons through itself
The balloons make oxygen that expands them
The enclosed volume increases, lowering pressure so air enters the balloons
The pressure inside the jar becomes greater than outside pressure
questions.explanation: Pulling the sheet down increases the surrounding volume. The pressure decrease lets outside air enter the balloons through the tube.

questions.prompt: Which is an important limitation of a simple bell-jar lung model?
options: It shows a volume change when the sheet moves
Air enters through a tube
The balloons can become larger
Its rigid jar does not show the movement of a real rib cage
questions.explanation: A rigid jar cannot represent rib movement and intercostal muscles. The model illustrates only some features of ventilation.

questions.prompt: In healthy lungs, which way does oxygen diffuse across the alveolar wall?
options: From alveolar air into capillary blood
From capillary blood into alveolar air only
From the tracheal cartilage into the bronchi
From the diaphragm into the ribs
questions.explanation: Oxygen diffuses from alveoli, where its concentration is higher, into the blood arriving in pulmonary capillaries.

questions.prompt: Which way does carbon dioxide normally diffuse at the alveoli?
options: From alveolar air into the blood only
From capillary blood into alveolar air
From the ribs into the trachea
From the heart valves into the bronchi
questions.explanation: Blood arriving at the lungs has more carbon dioxide than alveolar air, so carbon dioxide diffuses into the alveoli.

questions.prompt: Why are there so many alveoli in the lungs?
options: To make the diffusion barrier thicker
To replace the need for blood vessels
To provide a large total surface area for gas exchange
To store solid food until it is digested
questions.explanation: Many alveoli provide a very large surface area, supporting rapid diffusion of respiratory gases.

questions.prompt: Why are alveolar and capillary walls very thin?
options: To prevent any diffusion of oxygen
To increase the distance between air and blood
To allow air to flow through the veins as bubbles
To create a short diffusion distance
questions.explanation: The thin alveolar-capillary barrier gives gases a short path between air and blood.

questions.prompt: How does a good blood supply help alveolar gas exchange?
options: It brings carbon dioxide and carries oxygen away, maintaining concentration gradients
It stops oxygen from leaving the alveoli
It replaces alveolar air with liquid blood
It makes the alveolar walls thicker
questions.explanation: Continuous blood flow helps maintain gradients by supplying oxygen-poor blood and removing blood that has gained oxygen.

questions.prompt: How does ventilation help maintain oxygen diffusion into the blood?
options: It makes oxygen diffuse against its gradient
It refreshes alveolar air so its oxygen level remains relatively high
It seals every alveolus permanently
It stops blood reaching the lungs
questions.explanation: Ventilation replenishes oxygen in alveoli and removes carbon dioxide, helping maintain gradients for diffusion.

questions.prompt: Which change would usually slow gas exchange across an alveolar wall?
options: An increase in total functioning alveolar surface area
A greater oxygen concentration difference between air and blood
An increase in the thickness of the diffusion barrier
A shorter diffusion distance
questions.explanation: A thicker barrier gives gases a longer diffusion path and usually reduces the rate of exchange.

questions.prompt: Why is a moist alveolar surface useful?
options: It prevents all gases from moving
It turns nitrogen into oxygen
It makes the entire lung fill with water
Respiratory gases can dissolve before crossing the surface
questions.explanation: Gases dissolve in the thin moist lining before diffusing across the alveolar surface.

questions.prompt: An alveolus is ventilated normally but receives very little blood flow. What is the likely result?
options: Less oxygen can be transferred into circulating blood from that alveolus
More oxygen must enter the blood than normal
Gas exchange no longer needs a concentration gradient
All nearby bronchi become blood vessels
questions.explanation: Effective exchange needs both ventilation and perfusion. Poor blood flow limits how much oxygen can be carried away.

questions.prompt: Why does blood leave the lungs with more oxygen but less carbon dioxide than when it arrived?
options: Oxygen is converted into carbon dioxide inside the alveoli
The two gases diffuse in different directions down their own gradients
Carbon dioxide carries oxygen out of the blood
The pulmonary artery adds oxygen directly from the ribs
questions.explanation: Oxygen diffuses from alveolar air into blood while carbon dioxide diffuses from blood into alveoli. Each follows its own gradient.

questions.prompt: What is the difference between breathing and cellular respiration?
options: Breathing releases energy inside cells; respiration moves air
They are two names for exactly the same process
Breathing moves air; cellular respiration releases energy in cells
Respiration occurs only in the lungs and breathing only in muscles
questions.explanation: Breathing is ventilation. Cellular respiration is a set of chemical reactions in cells that release usable energy.

questions.prompt: Which word equation summarises aerobic respiration?
options: Carbon dioxide + water → glucose + oxygen
Glucose + carbon dioxide → oxygen + water
Oxygen + water → glucose + nitrogen
Glucose + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water
questions.explanation: Aerobic respiration uses glucose and oxygen and produces carbon dioxide and water, releasing energy in the process.

questions.prompt: Where does aerobic cellular respiration occur?
options: In living cells throughout the body
Only in the air inside the trachea
Only on the outside of the skin
Only in the blood plasma
questions.explanation: Many body cells carry out aerobic respiration. The lungs supply oxygen but are not the only site of respiration.

questions.prompt: Why does breathing rate usually increase during exercise?
options: Working muscles stop releasing energy
Working muscles need more oxygen and produce more carbon dioxide
Exercise turns all nitrogen into carbon dioxide
The lungs begin making glucose from oxygen
questions.explanation: Increased ventilation supports the greater gas-exchange demands of active, respiring muscles.

questions.prompt: Which combination usually increases the volume of air ventilated each minute during exercise?
options: A lower breathing rate and a smaller tidal volume
A smaller tidal volume with no change in breathing rate
A higher breathing rate and a larger tidal volume
No airflow and a higher heart rate
questions.explanation: Both more breaths per minute and deeper breaths can increase minute ventilation.

questions.prompt: A student takes 12 breaths per minute with a tidal volume of 0.5 L. What is minute ventilation?
options: 24 L/min
12.5 L/min
0.042 L/min
6 L/min
questions.explanation: Minute ventilation = breathing rate × tidal volume = 12 × 0.5 = 6 litres per minute.

questions.prompt: What does a minute ventilation of 8 litres per minute mean?
options: A total of 8 litres of air is moved into or out of the lungs each minute
Exactly 8 litres of oxygen is absorbed into the blood each minute
The person takes exactly 8 breaths each minute
The heart pumps exactly 8 litres of blood each minute
questions.explanation: Minute ventilation is the total volume of air moved into or out of the lungs each minute. Air is a mixture of gases, so this does not mean that 8 litres of oxygen is absorbed.

questions.prompt: Two students each ventilate 8 L of air per minute. One takes 10 breaths/min and the other 20 breaths/min. Which statement is correct?
options: Both students must have the same tidal volume
The first student has a larger tidal volume
The second student has a larger tidal volume
Neither student is moving air into the lungs
questions.explanation: For the same minute ventilation, fewer breaths require a larger volume per breath: 0.8 L compared with 0.4 L.

questions.prompt: Why can breathing stay faster than resting level for a while after vigorous exercise?
options: The muscles have permanently lost the ability to respire
The lungs are now producing glucose from nitrogen
Recovery processes still require oxygen and carbon dioxide removal
The diaphragm has become unable to relax
questions.explanation: Oxygen demand and carbon dioxide removal can remain elevated during recovery while the body returns towards resting conditions.

questions.prompt: Which observation most directly shows that exhaled air contains carbon dioxide?
options: It causes a glowing splint to relight strongly
It contains a greater percentage of oxygen than inhaled air
It has no water vapour
It turns limewater cloudy
questions.explanation: Carbon dioxide reacts with limewater to form a cloudy precipitate. Exhaled air contains more carbon dioxide than inhaled air.

questions.prompt: What is the function of mucus in the airways?
options: To trap particles and some pathogens
To make oxygen in the bronchi
To replace the diaphragm
To carry most oxygen to body cells
questions.explanation: Sticky mucus traps particles and pathogens, helping prevent them reaching the delicate gas-exchange surfaces.

questions.prompt: What do cilia in the airways do?
options: Pump blood around the lungs
Move mucus towards the throat
Produce all inhaled oxygen
Hold the rib bones together
questions.explanation: Cilia are tiny hair-like projections that beat to move mucus and trapped material towards the throat.

questions.prompt: Why can damage to airway cilia increase the risk of chest infections?
options: The lungs begin absorbing food instead of air
Red blood cells immediately stop being made
Mucus and trapped pathogens are cleared less effectively
The diaphragm no longer contains any muscle
questions.explanation: Damaged cilia reduce mucus clearance, allowing pathogens and particles to remain in the airways longer.

questions.prompt: How can emphysema reduce the efficiency of gas exchange?
options: It creates many extra intact alveoli
It makes the lungs produce oxygen
It replaces every bronchiole with a coronary artery
Damage to alveolar walls reduces the available surface area
questions.explanation: Emphysema damages alveolar walls and elastic tissue, reducing gas-exchange surface area and making exhalation harder.

questions.prompt: What commonly happens to airways during an asthma attack?
options: They narrow because of muscle tightening, inflammation and mucus
They become wider than normal with no inflammation
They turn into blood-filled capillaries
Their cartilage changes into red blood cells
questions.explanation: Asthma can narrow the airways through smooth-muscle contraction, inflammation and extra mucus, restricting airflow.

questions.prompt: Why can carbon monoxide exposure reduce oxygen transport?
options: It converts all alveoli into bronchi
Carbon monoxide binds strongly to haemoglobin
It acts as a normal substitute for oxygen in aerobic respiration
It makes the diaphragm grow a protective shell
questions.explanation: Carbon monoxide binds haemoglobin strongly, reducing the amount available to carry oxygen effectively.

questions.prompt: Which substance in tobacco smoke is strongly associated with dependence?
options: Haemoglobin
Glucose
Nicotine
Oxygen
questions.explanation: Nicotine is addictive. Other smoke constituents, including carcinogens and carbon monoxide, contribute to different health harms.

questions.prompt: A person has reduced alveolar surface area but normal movement of the ribs. Why might exercise still be difficult?
options: Normal rib movement guarantees unlimited oxygen uptake
The lungs no longer need any blood supply
Reduced surface area makes diffusion distance zero
Less gas-exchange capacity can limit oxygen delivery despite continued ventilation
questions.explanation: Ventilation and gas exchange are different processes. Normal chest movement cannot fully compensate for loss of exchange surface.

questions.prompt: Why should a breathing simulator not be used to diagnose asthma?
options: A teaching model cannot assess a person's symptoms or replace clinical tests
All wheezing is always caused by the same condition
Changing a slider measures real airway inflammation
A normal animation proves every user has healthy lungs
questions.explanation: Educational simulations illustrate mechanisms. Diagnosis requires appropriate medical assessment and, when indicated, clinical measurements.

questions.prompt: Why is avoiding smoking useful even though airways have protective mucus and cilia?
options: Cilia remove every carcinogen from smoke before it reaches any cell
The protective system can be damaged or overwhelmed and does not remove every harmful substance
Mucus makes carbon monoxide harmless in the blood
The presence of cilia prevents all lung disease
questions.explanation: Mucus and cilia provide partial protection, but smoke can damage them and contains gases and particles they cannot fully remove.

questions.prompt: A student counts 8 breaths in 30 seconds. What is the estimated breathing rate?
options: 8 breaths per minute
4 breaths per minute
16 breaths per minute
24 breaths per minute
questions.explanation: There are two 30-second intervals in a minute, so 8 × 2 = 16 breaths per minute.

questions.prompt: Which gas makes up the largest proportion of both inhaled and exhaled air?
options: Oxygen
Carbon dioxide
Hydrogen
Nitrogen
questions.explanation: Nitrogen is the largest component of inhaled and exhaled air. Exhaled air still contains nitrogen and a substantial amount of oxygen.

questions.prompt: Which statement about oxygen in exhaled air is correct?
options: Exhaled air still contains oxygen, but usually a smaller proportion than inhaled air
Exhaled air contains no oxygen at all
Exhaled air is pure oxygen
All inhaled oxygen is converted into nitrogen
questions.explanation: Only some inhaled oxygen is taken up by the blood. Exhaled air typically contains about 16% oxygen compared with about 21% in air.

questions.prompt: Which observation is consistent with exhaled air containing water vapour?
options: A glowing splint always relights
Condensation forms on a cool surface breathed onto
Limewater becomes completely dry
The nitrogen in the air turns blue
questions.explanation: Warm, moist exhaled air can cool on a surface and form liquid water droplets by condensation.

questions.prompt: In an investigation of exercise intensity and breathing rate, what should be the dependent variable?
options: The chosen exercise intensity
The type of stopwatch used
The measured breathing rate
The colour of the students' clothes
questions.explanation: The dependent variable is the measured response: breathing rate. Exercise intensity is the independent variable.

questions.prompt: Why should students use the same counting interval when comparing raw breath counts?
options: A longer counting interval always lowers the actual breathing rate
Breath counts are independent of measurement duration
A counting interval converts oxygen directly into energy
Different intervals can produce different counts even at the same breathing rate
questions.explanation: Counts depend on both rate and time. Use a standard interval or convert all measurements to breaths per minute.

questions.prompt: A breathing trace shows regular peaks getting farther apart. What does that suggest?
options: Breathing rate is decreasing
Breathing rate is increasing
Tidal volume must be exactly doubling
Oxygen has stopped diffusing into the blood
questions.explanation: A longer interval between successive breaths means fewer breaths per unit time. Peak spacing alone does not determine tidal volume.

questions.prompt: A breathing-volume trace has a larger peak-to-trough amplitude but the same spacing between breaths. What changed?
options: Breathing rate increased while tidal volume stayed similar
Tidal volume increased while breathing rate stayed similar
Both rate and volume must have fallen
No aspect of ventilation changed
questions.explanation: On a volume trace, greater peak-to-trough amplitude indicates larger breaths; unchanged spacing indicates a similar rate.

questions.prompt: Why can a model that shows moving air particles not by itself show the rate of gas diffusion into blood?
options: All air movement is the same process as diffusion across alveoli
There are no gas concentration differences in lungs
Ventilation moves air in bulk, while diffusion depends on gradients and the exchange barrier
Diffusion is caused only by the ribs moving
questions.explanation: Bulk air movement and molecular diffusion are distinct. Exchange rate also depends on surface area, distance, gradients and blood supply.

questions.prompt: A class finds faster breathing after exercise in one trial. What would strengthen the evidence?
options: Changing exercise type and timing for every trial
Ignoring results that differ from the prediction
Measuring only students with the expected result
Repeating controlled trials and using the same measurement method
questions.explanation: Repeated, controlled measurements help assess variability and support a more reliable conclusion without selecting only preferred results.
